title: The gambler's hymn
hookLine: a man swears off the slot machines, then hears the jingle. The Rig Veda keeps a gambler's own confession, and a Hindu answer: tend your field
carry: the householder's dharma: leave the dice, tend your field
tomorrow: what was there before anything at all?

cards: He promised. No more, not this time. He walks past the casino floor toward the exit, proud of himself.
Then, from behind a row of machines, comes the bright little jingle of someone winning. His feet slow. The promise was real, and so is the pull, and the pull is winning.
One Rig Veda hymn is spoken by a gambler, in his own voice, and it doesn't hold back.

teach.h: THE DICE THRILL HIM LIKE SOMA.
teach.b: He starts with the dice themselves. They thrill me, he says, in paraphrase, like a deep drink of soma. Then he tells what they cost.
My wife never quarreled with me, never got angry. She was kind to me and to my friends.

teach.h: HE DROVE AWAY A DEVOTED WIFE.
teach.b: And for the sake of one losing throw, I drove away a devoted wife. Now his mother-in-law hates him, his wife pushes him away, and his own family says: we don't know him, take him away. Then the line the hymn turns on.
When I decide I won't play, he says, I fall behind as my friends go off. But when the brown dice are thrown and their sound reaches me, off I go to the meeting place like a lover to a lover.
His resolve doesn't fail from lack of knowing better.
It fails at the sound. Then a voice cuts through. Don't play with dice.

teach.h: SAVITAR: DON'T PLAY. FARM YOUR FIELD.
teach.b: Farm your field. Be glad of what you have, and value it. There are your cattle, there is your wife.
So says Savitar, the god who rouses, linked with the sun. That's a real Hindu teaching, and an old one.

Life has room for wealth and pleasure, but inside dharma: the duty you owe the people who count on you. The householder's path is honest work, a home kept, a family cared for, and the dice break all three.
Hindus know where that road goes. The Mahabharata turns on a dice game, where Yudhishthira stakes his kingdom, his brothers, himself, and Draupadi.

how: The gambler's hymn is part of the Rig Veda's recited text. Hindu teachers point to Savitar's counsel in it, to leave the dice and tend one's field, and to the Mahabharata's dice game, as warnings against habits that wreck a household.

games.q: what does “what the rig veda is” mean?
o: hymns of praise, and even a gambler's confession
a list of lucky numbers for throwing dice
a rulebook for games played at royal courts

games.q: the gambler's hymn — tap the pairs.

s: the gambler's hymn praises the dice
the dice thrill him, but the hymn tells what they cost and ends with Savitar saying: don't play.
the gambler says his wife was kind and never quarreled
he says he drove away a devoted wife for one losing throw.
his resolve fails because he doesn't know better
he decides not to play, then the sound of the dice draws him back.

games.q: you're the gambler. you've promised yourself you're done. then you hear the brown dice thrown. what does the hymn say happens?
o: he goes to the meeting place like a lover.
he calls his wife for help.
games.why: he says when he decides not to play, he falls behind his friends, but at the sound of the dice off he goes, like a lover to a lover.

practice: Think of one pull that gets past your good intentions, a phone, a bet, an old argument, and without scolding yourself, notice its trigger. Then do what Savitar told the gambler: look at your field.
Name the people who count on you, one by one, and choose one small act of care for one of them today. If you pray, ask for strength in your own words.

wordCard.voice: What the Rig Veda is. Hymns of fire, dawn and the one called by many names, and also a gambler's confession, ending with Savitar's advice: farm your field.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a die, one of the dice. The gambler's hymn is sometimes called the akṣa sukta, the hymn of the dice.

carryVoice: Keep this one: the householder's dharma. Leave the dice, tend your field, care for the people at home. Tomorrow, a hymn that asks how everything began.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.34.1–5 (the dice delight like soma; a kind wife driven away for one throw; mother-in-law hates, family disowns; when I resolve not to play, the sound of the brown dice draws me back like a lover)
Rig Veda 10.34.10, 10.34.13 (the gambler's wife forlorn, his mother grieving; play not with dice, till your field, there are your cattle, there your wife: so says Savitar)
Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (the dice game: Yudhishthira stakes his kingdom, his brothers, himself and Draupadi)
